stages.title: General relativity and spacetime
stages.hook: Satellite navigation would drift by roughly ten kilometres a day without corrections from both special and general relativity. What does gravity do to time?
explain: General relativity (GR, Einstein 1915) replaces the Newtonian picture of a gravitational force by the idea that mass and energy curve spacetime, and free-falling bodies follow geodesics, the straightest possible paths in the curved geometry. It rests on the equivalence principle: locally, the effects of a uniform gravitational field cannot be distinguished from those of an accelerating frame, because inertial and gravitational mass are equal to high precision. The field equations are G_μν = (8πG ÷ c⁴) T_μν: spacetime curvature on the left, energy-momentum on the right.

For a non-rotating, uncharged spherical mass M the exterior solution is the Schwarzschild metric. Clocks at radius r tick slower than far-away clocks by the factor √(1 − 2GM ÷ rc²) ≈ 1 − GM ÷ rc² in the weak field, so lower clocks run slower and light climbing out is gravitationally redshifted. The Schwarzschild radius is R_s = 2GM ÷ c². Light passing the Sun's limb is deflected by 4GM ÷ (c²R) ≈ 1.75 arcseconds, twice the Newtonian value, confirmed by Eddington's 1919 eclipse expedition and later by radio interferometry. Mercury's perihelion advances by 43 arcseconds per century more than Newtonian planetary perturbations predict.

GPS satellites orbit at about 20 200 km altitude. Their clocks run faster than ground clocks by about 45.7 μs per day from weaker gravity and slower by about 7.2 μs per day from orbital speed (special relativity), a net gain of about 38.5 μs per day. Left uncorrected, this would give position errors growing by around 10 km per day. GR also predicts gravitational waves, black holes and the expansion of the universe, and it underpins modern cosmology.

example.q: Estimate how much faster a clock at GPS orbit radius (r = 2.657 × 10⁷ m) runs compared with one on Earth's surface (R = 6.371 × 10⁶ m) due to gravity alone, per day. Use GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s, weak-field approximation.

A force pulls it along a straight rope to the Sun

Space is empty so nothing acts on it

questions.q: Explain why GPS needs both special and general relativistic corrections and why the two corrections have opposite signs.
questions.model: Orbital speed makes satellite clocks run slower (special relativity, about −7 μs/day), while weaker gravity at altitude makes them run faster (general relativity, about +46 μs/day). The gravitational effect is larger, so the net is about +38 μs/day and must be corrected.

She is correct, since gravity needs mass to act on
Light is only affected by electric fields
Light has a small hidden mass that gravity pulls on
panel.why: In GR gravity is geometry, so all things including light follow the curved geometry, as confirmed by lensing.

panel.q: Why is the Newtonian prediction of light deflection by the Sun half of the GR value?
panel.model: For slow bodies only the time part of the metric matters, which matches Newtonian gravity. For light both the time and space parts of the curvature contribute equally, giving twice the Newtonian deflection.
panel.why: Space curvature adds an equal contribution for light.

panel.q: What does a singularity in a solution of GR (such as at r = 0 in the Schwarzschild solution) signal?
o: The breakdown of the classical theory, where quantum gravity is expected to matter
It marks a proven point of truly infinite density
It marks a location where time runs fastest
It is only an arithmetic error in the algebra
panel.why: Curvature diverges there and the equations cease to apply, indicating the need for a quantum theory of gravity.

teach.model: In general relativity mass curves spacetime, and clocks deeper in a gravitational well tick slower than clocks farther out. A GPS satellite clock runs about 46 microseconds a day faster than a ground clock because gravity is weaker up there, but about 7 microseconds slower because of its speed. The net is about 38 microseconds a day, which must be corrected.

stages.title: Quantum mechanics and quantum systems
stages.hook: An electron meets a barrier it classically cannot climb, yet it sometimes appears on the other side. How can a particle get through a wall?
explain: In quantum mechanics a system's state is a vector (wave function ψ) in a Hilbert space, observables are Hermitian operators, and measured values are their eigenvalues. Evolution follows the Schrödinger equation iħ ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ. The Born rule says |ψ|² is the probability density, so for a normalised state Σ|cᵢ|² = 1. Position and momentum operators do not commute, [x̂, p̂] = iħ, which leads to Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2.

Solvable systems include the infinite square well, E_n = n²π²ħ² ÷ (2mL²), and the harmonic oscillator, E_n = (n + ½)ħω, whose ground state has zero-point energy ½ħω. Hydrogen has E_n = −13.6 eV ÷ n². Spin-½ particles have two-component states; for a state (3/5)|↑⟩ + (4/5)|↓⟩ the probabilities of measuring up and down are 9/25 and 16/25. Measurement along one axis changes the state, and repeated identical preparations give a statistical spread.

Tunnelling occurs where the wave function decays within a classically forbidden region but remains non-zero after a finite barrier. For a rectangular barrier of height V and width L with E < V, T ≈ e^(−2κL) where κ = √(2m(V − E)) ÷ ħ. It powers nuclear fusion in stars, scanning tunnelling microscopes and tunnel diodes. Entangled states of two systems cannot be written as a product, and they show correlations exceeding the limits of local hidden-variable theories (Bell's theorem), as tested in experiments rewarded by the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics. Interpretations of measurement (Copenhagen, many-worlds and others) differ, but they give the same predictions.

example.q: An electron (E = 1 eV) meets a barrier of V = 2 eV and width L = 0.5 nm. Estimate the transmission probability using T ≈ e^(−2κL). Use m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, ħ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

misc.wrong: The wave function collapses because a conscious observer looks.
misc.right: Measurement requires interaction with a measuring apparatus. Whether and how collapse occurs depends on the interpretation, and no theory requires consciousness.

questions.q: The commutator [x̂, p̂] = iħ implies what?
o: Position and momentum cannot both have sharp values simultaneously
Position and momentum are always equal in size
Momentum is always zero for a bound particle
Measurements can be made without disturbing the system at all
questions.why: Non-commuting observables have no common eigenstates, giving the uncertainty relation Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2.

Halved, since the probability is proportional to 1/L
Doubled, since it grows with the width
Unchanged, because the energy is the same
questions.why: Doubling L doubles the exponent, so T becomes T².

questions.q: Which statement about the ground state of a harmonic oscillator is correct?
o: Its energy is ½ħω, not zero
Its energy is zero, so the oscillator is at rest
Its energy is ħω, one full quantum
It has no wave function until it is measured
questions.why: Zero-point energy ½ħω follows from E_n = (n + ½)ħω and the uncertainty principle.

questions.q: A hydrogen atom is in an energy eigenstate. What will repeated energy measurements on the same state give?
o: The same value each time
A random value each time
Zero
Values that always increase
questions.why: Measuring an observable on one of its eigenstates yields the corresponding eigenvalue with certainty.

Passing through a classically forbidden barrier
questions.why: These are standard terms in quantum theory.

questions.q: Explain why Bell-test violations rule out local hidden-variable theories but do not allow faster-than-light messaging.
questions.model: Entangled measurements show correlations stronger than any local hidden-variable theory can give, as in violations of Bell inequalities. But each party's individual outcomes are random, so no usable message is transmitted without a classical channel to compare results.
questions.why: Correlations are not controllable signals.

questions.q: Order the steps in a quantum measurement of spin along a chosen axis.
items: Prepare the system in a state
Repeat many times to build a probability distribution
questions.why: Quantum predictions are statistical, confirmed over many identical preparations.

panel.q: A student says: 'Tunnelling means the particle borrows energy and breaks energy conservation.' What is the best reply?
o: No: the particle's wave function extends into the barrier, and its total energy is well defined and conserved
Yes, it breaks the law for a very short time
Tunnelling is only a measurement error in the detector
Energy is not defined at all in quantum mechanics
panel.why: The energy eigenvalue is fixed; the classical notion of a particle with definite position and kinetic energy inside the barrier does not apply.

panel.q: Why does the probability of finding an electron at any location depend on |ψ|² and not on ψ?
panel.model: ψ is generally complex-valued and may be negative, so it cannot be a probability. The squared magnitude |ψ|² is real and non-negative, and the Born rule identifies it as the probability density.
panel.why: Probabilities must be real and non-negative.

panel.q: Two electrons in a singlet state are measured along the same axis far apart. What is guaranteed?
o: Opposite spin outcomes
Identical spin outcomes every time
Both spins always come out up
No correlation between the two outcomes
panel.why: The singlet has total spin zero, so measurements along the same axis give opposite results, although each is individually random.

teach.model: In quantum mechanics a particle is described by a wave function. Inside a barrier the wave does not drop to zero at once but fades away exponentially. If the barrier is thin enough, some of the wave reaches the other side, so there is a small chance of finding the particle there. For example, an electron meeting a 0.5 nm barrier has about a 0.6% chance of passing.

stages.title: Cosmology and the early universe
stages.hook: The sky glows faintly with microwaves from every direction at a temperature of 2.7 kelvin. What is this glow, and what does it say about the first few hundred thousand years?
explain: The standard cosmological model (ΛCDM) is built on the cosmological principle, that on large scales the universe is homogeneous and isotropic, and on GR. The metric is Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker, with scale factor a(t). Redshift measures expansion: 1 + z = a₀ ÷ a. Hubble's law v = H₀d holds at low redshift, with H₀ ≈ 67–73 km/s/Mpc (the measurements from the early universe and local distance ladder differ, the 'Hubble tension'). The Friedmann equation H² = (8πG ÷ 3)ρ − kc²/a² + Λc²/3 links expansion to content; the critical density is ρ_c = 3H² ÷ (8πG) ≈ 9 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/m³ for H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc.

Observations show a flat universe made of about 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter and 68% dark energy. Evidence for a hot early phase includes the abundance of light elements from Big Bang nucleosynthesis (about 25% helium-4 by mass, formed in the first few minutes) and the cosmic microwave background (CMB). The CMB was released at recombination, when the universe was about 380 000 years old, at z ≈ 1100 and T ≈ 3000 K. It has since cooled as T = 2.725 K × (1 + z). Its tiny temperature fluctuations (about 10⁻⁵) record the seeds of galaxies.

Cosmic inflation, a brief epoch of exponential expansion in the first fraction of a second, is proposed to explain the flatness and horizon problems and to generate the primordial fluctuations; it is well motivated but not directly confirmed. The universe's age from the best fits is about 13.8 billion years; a rough estimate is 1 ÷ H₀, about 14 billion years for H₀ = 70.

example.q: Estimate the critical density for H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc. Use 1 Mpc = 3.086 × 10²² m and G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².
example.a: About 9 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/m³ (about 5 hydrogen atoms per cubic metre)

Hubble's space telescope has broken down
H₀ is found to equal zero
The universe is found not to be expanding

panel.q: Why do cosmologists use the CMB's tiny fluctuations of about 1 part in 10⁵ to infer the composition of the universe?
panel.model: Before recombination, photons and baryons oscillated as sound waves in gravitational wells. The positions and heights of the acoustic peaks in the angular power spectrum depend on the geometry and on the densities of baryons, dark matter and dark energy.
panel.why: The fluctuation spectrum encodes the physics of the early plasma.

panel.q: If the universe's expansion rate were constant, 1/H₀ would give its age exactly. Why is the actual age (13.8 Gyr) slightly less than 1/H₀ ≈ 14 Gyr for H₀ = 70?
o: Expansion decelerated in the matter-dominated era and then accelerated, so 1/H₀ is only approximate
The universe is shrinking, which reduces the age
H₀ is wrong by a factor of 2
Time does not flow uniformly, so no age can be found
panel.why: The history of H(t) differs from constant, so the exact age depends on the contents; for ΛCDM it comes out at about 0.96/H₀.

teach.topic: What the cosmic microwave background is
teach.model: About 380 000 years after the Big Bang the universe cooled enough for electrons and nuclei to form atoms, and light could finally travel freely. That light has been stretched by the expansion of space ever since, from about 3000 K to 2.725 K, so we see it today as microwaves from all directions. For example, its tiny ripples show where galaxies would later form.

stages.title: Black holes and gravitational waves
stages.hook: On 14 September 2015 two detectors in the United States registered a distortion only a few thousandths of a proton's width. What had they heard?
explain: A black hole is a region from which nothing, not even light, can escape. In GR a non-rotating black hole is described by the Schwarzschild solution, with an event horizon at R_s = 2GM ÷ c² (2.95 km per solar mass). Rotating holes (Kerr) have an ergosphere and an innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) that for a Schwarzschild hole lies at 6GM ÷ c² = 3R_s. Black holes are characterised by mass, spin and charge only (the no-hair idea). Stellar-mass holes form from collapsed massive stars; supermassive holes of 10⁶–10¹⁰ M☉ sit in galaxy centres, such as about 4 million M☉ at the centre of the Milky Way (Sagittarius A*) and 6.5 billion M☉ in M87.

Hawking showed that black holes radiate thermally with T = ħc³ ÷ (8πGMk_B), about 6 × 10⁻⁸ K for a solar mass, far colder than the CMB, so the effect is negligible for astrophysical holes. The Event Horizon Telescope produced the first image of a black hole's shadow in M87 (2019) and of Sagittarius A* (2022).

Accelerating masses emit gravitational waves, ripples of spacetime travelling at c. They carry energy, and the strain h is the fractional change in length. LIGO's 4 km arms detected GW150914, the merger of black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses into one of about 62 solar masses, radiating about 3 solar masses of energy in a fraction of a second. For a binary, the gravitational wave frequency is twice the orbital frequency, and it rises as the orbit shrinks (a chirp). Neutron star mergers (GW170817) were seen in both gravitational waves and light, which led to measuring the speed of gravity and the origin of heavy elements.

example.q: A gravitational wave of strain h = 1.0 × 10⁻²¹ passes through a detector with arms of length 4.0 km. By how much does the difference in arm lengths change? Use ΔL = hL.
example.a: About 4 × 10⁻¹⁸ m, a few thousandths of a proton's diameter

Earth is pulled into the black hole at once
Earth flies away in a straight line
Earth orbits faster because of the stronger gravity

She speeds up beyond the speed of light and vanishes
She disappears instantly as she crosses
She bounces back off the horizon
questions.why: Signals from near the horizon take longer and lose energy, so the image fades and reddens.

It is hotter than the Sun, so the hole loses mass fast
It has been observed and measured directly
It does not depend on the mass of the hole
questions.why: T ≈ 6 × 10⁻⁸ K is far below 2.7 K, so absorption of CMB photons dominates.

The detector is drifting out of calibration
The black holes gain mass quickly as they merge
The distance to the source decreases rapidly

Neutron-star merger seen in gravitational waves and light
Image of the shadow of M87*
Stars orbiting a compact object of about 4 million M☉
questions.why: These are landmark observations in black-hole astrophysics.

questions.q: Explain how an interferometer such as LIGO detects a gravitational wave and why the arms are so long.
questions.model: A gravitational wave stretches one arm while squeezing the other. Laser beams travelling down the two arms recombine, and the tiny path-length change shifts the interference pattern. Because the change is ΔL = hL, a longer arm gives a bigger absolute change, which improves sensitivity to the very small strain.
questions.why: Interference converts a tiny differential length change into a measurable light signal.

questions.q: Order the phases of a binary black hole merger signal.
questions.why: The binary spirals together, merges, and the final hole settles with ringing.

panel.q: Gravitational waves from GW170817 and a gamma-ray burst arrived within about 1.7 seconds after travelling about 130 million light-years. What does this show?
o: Gravity travels at the speed of light to a precision of about 10⁻¹⁵
Gravity travels much faster than light
Light travels much faster than gravity

stages.title: Dark matter and dark energy
stages.hook: Everything we can see, from stars to gas, makes up only about 5% of the universe's energy budget. How do we know the rest is there?
explain: Evidence for dark matter comes from several independent observations: flat galaxy rotation curves, velocity dispersions of galaxies in clusters (Zwicky 1933), gravitational lensing, the Bullet Cluster where the lensing mass is offset from the hot gas, the CMB acoustic peaks, and the formation of large-scale structure. A rough mass estimate for a bound system is M ≈ v²R ÷ G. Candidates include weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), axions and primordial black holes, but none has been detected despite sensitive underground experiments. Alternatives such as modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) fit many rotation curves but struggle with clusters and the CMB.

Dark energy was discovered in 1998 when observations of distant Type Ia supernovae by two teams (Riess, Schmidt and Perlmutter received the 2011 Nobel Prize) showed that the expansion of the universe is accelerating. In the Friedmann acceleration equation, ä ÷ a = −(4πG ÷ 3)(ρ + 3p ÷ c²), acceleration requires a component with equation of state w = p ÷ (ρc²) < −1/3. The simplest candidate is the cosmological constant Λ, with w = −1 and constant energy density; others, such as quintessence, have w varying in time.

Components dilute differently as the universe expands: matter ρ ∝ a⁻³, radiation ρ ∝ a⁻⁴ and a cosmological constant ρ ∝ a⁰. This is why radiation dominated first, then matter, and dark energy now dominates, with Ω_m ≈ 0.31 and Ω_Λ ≈ 0.69 today (about 5%, 27% and 68% for ordinary matter, dark matter and dark energy respectively). If w = −1 holds, the universe will expand ever faster and structures outside gravitationally bound groups will recede beyond view. Whether Λ is truly constant is being tested by surveys such as DESI and Euclid.

stages.title: Computational astrophysics
stages.hook: No equation can predict the orbits of three stars for all time, yet astronomers simulate whole galaxies. How can a computer be trusted when it only gives approximations?
explain: Most astrophysical problems have no closed-form solution, so we integrate the equations numerically. The simplest scheme is explicit (forward) Euler: x_{n+1} = x_n + v_nΔt, v_{n+1} = v_n + a_nΔt. It is first-order accurate, and for oscillating or orbiting systems it gradually adds energy (for a harmonic oscillator each step multiplies the energy by 1 + ω²Δt²). The leapfrog (Verlet) method is second-order and symplectic: it keeps the energy error bounded for long runs, which is why it is the standard in N-body codes.

Gravity between N bodies needs N(N − 1)/2 pair forces by direct summation, a cost of O(N²). Tree codes (Barnes–Hut) group distant particles and cost O(N log N), and particle-mesh methods use fast Fourier transforms. To avoid unphysically large forces in close encounters, a softening length ε replaces r² with r² + ε². The time step must resolve the shortest dynamical timescale, often by a fraction of the orbital period, and many codes use adaptive steps. Hydrodynamics uses grids (finite volume) or smoothed particles (SPH).

Good practice means verifying and validating. Verification checks that the code solves the equations correctly: test conserved quantities (energy, momentum, angular momentum), convergence when the step is reduced (error ∝ Δtᵖ for an order-p method), and known analytic cases such as a Kepler orbit. Validation compares with observations. Monte Carlo methods estimate integrals by random sampling with error ∝ 1/√N. Floating-point arithmetic has finite precision (double precision about 16 digits), so round-off errors accumulate, and reproducibility needs recorded software versions, random seeds and open data.

stages.title: Advanced orbital dynamics
stages.hook: To reach geostationary orbit a spacecraft needs far less speed change than to leave the Solar System. How can orbital energy tell us the cost of any transfer?
explain: For a Keplerian orbit about a mass M with semi-major axis a, the specific orbital energy is ε = −GM ÷ 2a, which is negative for bound orbits. The vis-viva equation v² = GM(2/r − 1/a) gives the speed at any radius r. Circular orbits have r = a so v = √(GM/r); escape requires ε ≥ 0, so v_esc = √(2GM/r) = √2 v_circ. The orbital period is T = 2π√(a³ ÷ GM). For Earth GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²; for the Sun GM = 1.327 × 10²⁰ m³/s².

A Hohmann transfer between coplanar circular orbits of radii r₁ and r₂ is an ellipse with a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 touching both. Two burns are needed: Δv₁ at r₁ to enter the ellipse and Δv₂ at r₂ to circularise, and the transfer lasts half the ellipse's period. From a 300 km low Earth orbit (r₁ = 6.678 × 10⁶ m) to geostationary orbit (r₂ = 4.216 × 10⁷ m), Δv₁ ≈ 2.43 km/s, Δv₂ ≈ 1.47 km/s, total ≈ 3.9 km/s and the transfer takes about 5.3 hours. Gravity assists exchange momentum with a planet: in the planet's frame the speed is unchanged but the direction changes, so in the Sun's frame the spacecraft can gain up to about twice the planet's orbital speed.

The two-body problem is exactly solvable, but three bodies are not in general. The restricted three-body problem has five Lagrange points. L1, L2 and L3 are saddle points (unstable), while L4 and L5 are stable for mass ratios below about 0.0385 (Earth–Sun, Earth–Moon, Sun–Jupiter pairs satisfy this). The Sun–Earth L1 and L2 lie about 1.5 million km from Earth and host solar observatories and the James Webb Space Telescope (L2). Real orbits are perturbed by Earth's oblateness (J₂), which causes nodal precession used by sun-synchronous orbits, by drag at low altitude, by third bodies and by solar radiation pressure.

stages.title: Astrophysical fluid dynamics
stages.hook: Interstellar gas is a million times thinner than the best laboratory vacuum on Earth, yet it still behaves as a fluid. When can we treat dust, gas and plasma as a continuous flow?
explain: Astrophysical fluids obey the Euler or Navier–Stokes equations coupled to gravity: continuity ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρv) = 0, momentum ρ(∂v/∂t + v·∇v) = −∇P − ρ∇Φ + viscous and magnetic terms, plus an energy equation. A fluid description holds when the mean free path is much shorter than the length scale of interest; in plasmas magnetic fields shorten the effective scale. In hydrostatic equilibrium dP/dr = −ρg, which sets the structure of stars and planetary atmospheres. The sound speed is c_s = √(γk_BT ÷ μm_H); for fully ionised hydrogen at 10⁴ K (γ = 5/3, μ = 0.5) it is about 16.6 km/s. A flow with Mach number M = v ÷ c_s greater than 1 is supersonic and develops shocks, as in supernova remnants.

The Reynolds number Re = ρvL ÷ μ measures inertia against viscosity; astrophysical flows have Re ≫ 1 and are turbulent. Gravitational collapse of a gas cloud occurs when it exceeds the Jeans length λ_J ≈ c_s √(π ÷ Gρ): larger clouds cannot be supported by pressure, which is how stars begin to form. In a magnetised plasma, the Alfvén speed v_A = B ÷ √(μ₀ρ) is the speed of magnetic waves; for B = 10⁻⁹ T (10 μG) and ρ = 1.67 × 10⁻²¹ kg/m³ (about 1 hydrogen atom per cm³) it is about 22 km/s. Magnetic fields are 'frozen in' to highly conducting plasma, and can twist, reconnect and release energy (as in solar flares).

Accretion powers many luminous sources. Matter with angular momentum forms a disc, and viscosity (probably from magnetorotational turbulence) transports angular momentum outwards so gas can fall inwards. The accretion luminosity is L = η ṁ c², where η ≈ 0.1 is a typical value for black-hole discs (about 0.06 for a non-spinning hole, higher for a rapidly spinning one). Radiation pressure limits steady spherical accretion: the Eddington luminosity L_Edd = 4πGMm_pc ÷ σ_T ≈ 1.26 × 10³¹ W × (M/M☉), about 3 × 10⁴ L☉ per solar mass. Other instabilities include Rayleigh–Taylor (a heavy fluid above a light one), Kelvin–Helmholtz (shear) and convection when the temperature gradient is steeper than the adiabatic one.

questions.q: A gas cloud has higher temperature, other things equal. What happens to its Jeans length?
o: It increases, making collapse harder
It decreases, making collapse easier
It stays the same whatever the temperature
It becomes zero, so the cloud collapses at once
questions.why: λ_J ∝ c_s ∝ √T, so a hotter cloud needs more mass to collapse.

questions.q: What is the Reynolds number of a flow with ρ = 1 kg/m³, v = 1 m/s, L = 1 m and viscosity μ = 10⁻⁵ Pa·s?
questions.why: Re = ρvL ÷ μ = 1 ÷ 10⁻⁵ = 10⁵, firmly in the turbulent regime.

questions.q: In hydrostatic equilibrium in a star, what balances the inward gravitational pull?
o: A pressure gradient pointing outward
Magnetic monopoles inside the star
Centrifugal force from the star's surface
Dark energy pushing from outside
questions.why: dP/dr = −ρg means pressure decreases outward with enough gradient to support the layer's weight.

questions.q: Why does an accretion disc form around a compact object instead of gas falling straight in?
o: Infalling gas has angular momentum and cannot fall in until that is transported outward
Gas is repelled by the compact object
The black hole has no gravity at all
Discs are only an artist's painting
questions.why: Conservation of angular momentum makes gas orbit; viscosity (turbulence) transfers angular momentum outward, allowing slow inflow.

questions.q: Match each instability or process to its trigger.
questions.why: Each is a distinct source of instability in astrophysical flows.

questions.q: Explain how the Eddington luminosity arises and why it limits the brightness of steady spherical accretion.
questions.model: Photons scatter off free electrons (Thomson scattering) and push the plasma outward. At the Eddington luminosity this outward radiation force balances the inward gravitational pull on protons and electrons. Above it, radiation would expel the infalling gas, limiting steady spherical accretion to L ≲ L_Edd.
questions.why: Both forces scale as 1/r², so the balance gives a luminosity depending only on mass.

questions.q: Order these speeds in a molecular cloud complex from slowest to fastest.
items: Sound speed in cold gas (0.2 km/s)
questions.why: Numerically, the sound speed 0.2 < turbulence 1 < Alfvén 2 < blast wave 1000 km/s.

panel.q: The Alfvén speed is v_A = B ÷ √(μ₀ρ). If the density of a plasma is quadrupled at fixed B, v_A...
o: Halves
Doubles
Quadruples
Stays the same
panel.why: v_A ∝ 1/√ρ, so quadrupling ρ halves it.

panel.q: Why does magnetic reconnection in the solar corona release energy quickly, even though a highly conducting plasma freezes field lines into the flow?
panel.model: Where oppositely directed field lines are pushed together, thin current sheets form and the frozen-in condition breaks down locally. Field lines reconnect into a lower-energy configuration, releasing magnetic energy as heat, bulk flow and accelerated particles.
panel.why: Freezing-in fails in thin current sheets, allowing a change of topology.

panel.q: A gas cloud has a sound speed of 0.2 km/s and a stirring speed of 2 km/s. What is the Mach number and its implication?
o: 10, supersonic turbulence that makes shocks and dense filaments
0.1, subsonic and smooth
1, exactly sonic with no shocks
100, a relativistic flow
panel.why: M = 2 ÷ 0.2 = 10; supersonic turbulence compresses gas into shocks and filaments where stars may form.

teach.topic: Why a cloud of gas in space can collapse to form stars
teach.model: Gas pressure pushes outward while gravity pulls inward. In a cold, dense and large enough cloud, gravity wins and the cloud collapses. The critical size is the Jeans length, which grows with the sound speed. So a cloud that is cooler, denser or heavier collapses more easily.

points.ask: What resists the collapse?
What drives the collapse?
How do we know when gravity wins?
What helps a cloud collapse?

stages.title: Integrated cosmic research mission
stages.hook: You lead a team that has just found a faint dip repeating every 10 days in the light of a nearby red dwarf. Which measurements, in what order, would turn that dip into a characterised world?
explain: This capstone combines methods from the whole world: measurement and uncertainty, orbital mechanics, radiation, stellar physics, detection methods and communication. The target is a red dwarf with mass 0.40 M☉, radius 0.40 R☉ and temperature 3300 K. A transit of depth 1.00 ± 0.05% recurs every 10.0 days. Step one is stellar characterisation: from L = 4πR²σT⁴ in solar units, L ≈ (0.40)²(3300 ÷ 5772)⁴ L☉ ≈ 0.017 L☉.

Step two is the orbit: Kepler's third law in AU, years and solar masses gives a³ = M T², so a³ = 0.40 × (10.0 ÷ 365.25)² = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ and a ≈ 0.067 AU. Step three is size: depth = (R_p ÷ R_*)², so R_p ÷ R_* = 0.100 and R_p = 0.040 R☉ ≈ 2.8 × 10⁷ m ≈ 4.4 R⊕ (a sub-Neptune size). Step four is thermal: T_eq = T_*√(R_* ÷ 2a)(1 − A)^¼; for A = 0 this gives about 390 K, far hotter than Earth's 255 K, so surface liquid water would need a very reflective atmosphere and cannot be judged without more data. Step five is mass from radial velocity, giving density and composition.

Throughout, scientific practice matters: propagate uncertainty (a 5% error on depth gives a 2.5% error on radius ratio because R_p ∝ √depth), check for false positives such as eclipsing binaries, verify with independent instruments, use blinded analysis where possible, share data and code, and allow peer review. Claims about habitability or life are claims about probability, and extraordinary claims need multiple independent lines of evidence. Communicating limits honestly is part of the science.

example.q: The star's flux measured at Earth is 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ W/m² and L = 6.5 × 10²⁴ W. Find the distance in parsecs. Use d = √(L ÷ 4πF) and 1 pc = 3.086 × 10¹⁶ m.
steps: d = 2.27 × 10¹⁷ ÷ 3.086 × 10¹⁶ ≈ 7.4 pc (a parallax of about 0.136 arcsec).

analogies.home: Detectives combine fingerprints, timing and witness statements; a planet needs several independent measurements.
analogies.city: City planners use traffic counts, maps and surveys together before a decision.
analogies.sea: Navigators combine compass, speed and star sights, checking one method against another.
analogies.tech: Engineers combine unit tests, integration tests and field trials before launching a product.

stages.mnemonic: Characterise the star, find the orbit, size the planet, estimate temperature, weigh it, then challenge your own result.
terms: The planet's temperature from the balance of absorbed and emitted radiation, ignoring greenhouse warming.
Calculating the uncertainty of a result from the uncertainties of its inputs.
A signal that mimics a planet but has another cause.

misc.wrong: One dataset showing a promising feature establishes a discovery.
misc.right: Discovery claims need independent confirmation, careful treatment of uncertainty and exclusion of alternative explanations.

stages.limits: Equilibrium temperature ignores the greenhouse effect, internal heat and atmospheric circulation, and masses from radial velocity are minimum masses unless inclination is known. Red dwarf planets may face flares and tidal locking.

trip.prompt: Find how transit, timing and radial velocity data were combined to characterise the system's planets.

questions.q: Using a³ = M T² (AU, years, solar masses), find the orbital distance in AU for a planet with a 10.0-day period around a 0.40 M☉ star. Give the answer to three decimal places.
The transit depth is 1.00% with an uncertainty of 0.05% (absolute). What is the fractional uncertainty in the radius ratio R_p ÷ R_* = √depth, in percent?
questions.why: The depth has a 5% relative error; for a square root the relative error halves, giving 2.5%.

questions.q: A star has R = 0.40 R☉ and T = 3300 K. Using L = R²T⁴ in solar units (T☉ = 5772 K), roughly what is L?
The transit depth is 1.0%. What is the planet's radius relative to its star's?
A dip of 1% is seen, but later images show a faint eclipsing binary lying within the same pixel. What does this indicate?
o: A possible false positive that must be ruled out
A confirmed planet, with no further checks needed
A satellite passing across the field of view
A calibration success for the telescope
questions.why: Blended eclipsing binaries can mimic transit signals and must be excluded by follow-up imaging and spectroscopy.

questions.q: The planet has an equilibrium temperature of about 390 K for zero albedo. Which statement is best?
o: Surface liquid water cannot be concluded without atmosphere and albedo data
It definitely has oceans on its surface
It definitely has no atmosphere around it
Temperature has no relation to liquid water
questions.why: Equilibrium temperature is a first estimate; actual conditions depend on albedo, atmosphere and pressure.

questions.q: A signal from a probe at 7.4 pc (about 24 light-years) is sent today. When can it be received?
o: In about 24 years
In about 2.4 years
At once
In about 240 years
questions.why: Electromagnetic signals travel at c, so they take as many years as the distance in light-years.

questions.q: Match each measurement to the quantity it provides.
pairs: Transit period with Kepler's third law
questions.why: Each is a step in characterising the system.

questions.q: A colleague proposes announcing 'a habitable planet found' based on the equilibrium temperature alone. Write a short, critical evaluation using at least two scientific reasons.
questions.model: Equilibrium temperature ignores atmosphere, albedo and greenhouse effects, so it cannot show liquid water. The planet's radius of about 4 Earth radii suggests a gas-rich sub-Neptune rather than a rocky planet, and mass and composition are unknown. The claim needs independent confirmation, follow-up atmospheric spectra and consideration of flares and tidal locking, so it is premature.
questions.why: Habitability claims need several lines of evidence.

questions.q: Order a sensible sequence for this research programme.
items: Rule out false positives with follow-up imaging and spectroscopy
Derive orbit, radius and equilibrium temperature
Measure mass with radial velocities and plan atmospheric observations
questions.why: Confirm the signal is real before interpreting it, then characterise step by step.

panel.q: A reviewer asks you to show that your radius result does not depend on analysis choices. Which practice best addresses this?
o: Repeat the analysis with different reasonable methods and report the spread, sharing data and code
Use only the method that gives the nicest answer
Delete outlying points without telling anyone
Cite your own previous work as proof
panel.why: Systematic uncertainty is tested by varying analysis choices transparently, and openness enables independent checks.

panel.q: Why is the star's own radius uncertainty important when you quote the planet's radius?
panel.model: The transit gives only the ratio R_p ÷ R_*, so the planet's radius is that ratio times the stellar radius. Any error in the stellar radius carries straight into the planet radius and must be combined with the depth uncertainty.
panel.why: R_p = (R_p ÷ R_*) × R_*, so errors propagate.

panel.q: If the planet were found to have a density of 1.6 g/cm³, which is closer to Neptune (1.6 g/cm³) than to Earth (5.5 g/cm³), what would you infer?
o: A substantial volatile envelope, not a bare rocky world
A solid ball made mostly of iron
A pure rock planet like Earth
A small star
panel.why: Low bulk density needs a large fraction of light material such as hydrogen, helium or water.

teach.topic: How to characterise a newly found transiting planet
teach.model: First measure the star: its radius, temperature and mass. The depth of the dip gives the planet's size relative to its star, and the time between dips gives its orbit using Kepler's third law. From the star's temperature and the distance we can estimate the planet's temperature. Then radial-velocity data give its mass. We always check for false positives and quote the uncertainties.

What does the dip tell you?
How do you find its orbit?
How do you make sure the result is right?
